Prosecution first. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours. In 1993, after his forces had radically altered the demographic picture in the portions of Bosnia claimed by the Bosnian Serbs, Ratko Mladic took credit for what had been done under his command and for the positive situation in which Bosnian Serb negotiators now found themselves. "Mr. President, you have started from the most favourable starting position in Geneva. You had the military result in your hands." P2508, pages 32 through 33, and may the Court Officer be instructed, please, to show the Sanction presentation on the large screens. That military result, Your Honours, was the realisation of a strategy to create a factual situation that could not be reversed, a reconfiguration of Bosnian demographics that the international community - as well as Muslims and Croats - would have to accept as permanent. It didn't happen secretly, as Karadzic quoted a Bosnian Serb War Commissioner: "We are skinning the cat alive before the whole world." P4584, pages 13 and 15. As the entire world was able to see, what had happened in municipality after municipality was not an unintended effect of the military campaign but its very purpose. UN Special Rapporteur Mazowiecki reported in August 1992: "Ethnic cleansing does not appear to be the consequence of the war, but rather its goal. This goal, to a large extent, has already been achieved through killings, beatings, rape, destruction of houses and threats." It's P2813, paragraph 6. By the time that the Special Rapporteur made these observations, General Mladic's VRS controlled approximately 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You can find that at P4581, pages 38, 48, and 55. By the summer of 1992, they had enough to be thinking about cease-fires and freezing their already advantageous positions. P3113, pages 1, 3, and 5. Offers of cease-fire, however, did not mean that their territorial objectives had been fully satisfied, as reflected, for example, in General Mladic's November 1992 Directive 4, which orders the VRS to pursue an as-yet unfulfilled Strategic Objective, number 3, by forcing the enemy "with the Muslim population" to leave Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas. It's P2217, page 5. Those Eastern Bosnia operations continued, in Karadzic's words "packing Muslims in small areas." P4584, page 13, and culminated - temporarily at any rate - when the international community prevented their take-over of Srebrenica and established safe areas. As General Mladic said: "If the international community had not meddled, they," meaning the Muslims, "would have paid the price for everything they had done up to then to the Serb people." P1973, page 5. Despite this setback, the focus on Srebrenica and the remaining enclaves persisted. As General Mladic communicated to the Drina Corps in 1994, which was captured in an information report to the Bratunac Brigade and this is from the report: "We must attain our final goal, an entirely Serbian Podrinje," and that report continued, "we must continue to arm, train, discipline, and prepare the RS Army for the execution of this crucial task: The expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave." That's P1505, page 3, also found at the transcript 111786 through 90. As General Mladic explained in 1994 to the Bosnian Serb Assembly, the Bosnian Serbs had a historical opportunity to create "not any kind of state, but an all-Serbian state ... with ... as little enemies as possible, those who could be our potential enemies and raise against us in a few years ..." His concern, he told the Assembly was not that Muslims might create a state. His concern "is to have them vanish completely." P3076, pages 18 through 20. By March 1995, General Mladic and Radovan Karadzic re-intensified their focus on Srebrenica, issuing a directive to create conditions to make the lives of Srebrenica's inhabitants "unbearable." That's Directive 7. By July 2nd a combat operation in furtherance of Directive 7 was underway. On the 9th of July, General Mladic and Karadzic realised they could take the enclave itself and changed the operations to do so. On the 11th of July, General Mladic walked into Srebrenica and vowed that the time had come to take revenge on the Turks. That's P1147, page 11. Within a short time, over 7.000 Srebrenica men and boys, boys as young as 12, had been systematically murdered and all of the remaining inhabitants of Srebrenica expelled. The Srebrenica community had been destroyed, had "vanished." Meanwhile, Bosnia's capital had been held under what General Mladic called "our hammer." P431, page 35. Its civilian population subjected to a campaign of shelling and sniping that was increased to place pressure on or retaliate against the Muslim side or, conversely, reduced in response to pressures from the international community. Internationals who arrived at different points in the conflict came to the same conclusion, that the primary purpose of the shelling and sniping was to induce terror in the civilian population. The campaign was so pervasive and enduring that life itself in Sarajevo, including even the behaviour of children, painfully adapted to it. The effort to produce terror through shelling and sniping was also buttressed by the simultaneous pressure of restrictions on humanitarian aid and basic means of life: Water, heating, electricity. These massive criminal efforts - municipalities, Sarajevo, Srebrenica - along with the taking of UN personnel as hostages in May 1995 in order to prevent NATO air-strikes, these efforts are reflected in four separate but related JCEs charged in the indictment, all distinct, although each broadly in service of the same goal of achieving a Serbian state on vast territories within Bosnia-Herzegovina with as few historical enemies as possible. Your Honours, by way of presentation I will be discussing with you aspects of the overarching JCE in the context of addressing claims made in the Defence final trial brief. Mr. Traldi will then address General Mladic's implementation of the common purpose, the overarching common purpose. I will then return to speak about Count 1, genocide, in the municipalities, specifically focussing as we did on our brief on the municipality of Prijedor. Mr. Weber will then address the Sarajevo, the terror JCE; followed by Mr. McCloskey on the elimination JCE in Srebrenica in July 1995, the execution of over 7.000 men and boys and the forceable transfer of the women, children, and elderly. Finally, Your Honours, I will address you on sentencing. More specifically with respect to my remarks this morning, I will be addressing claims in the Defence brief related to the overarching JCE, claims that the common purpose or General Mladic's contributions to it are belied by such things as local autonomy in the municipalities, or no plans by the leadership, or the alleged fact that those who left were welcome to come back, or by General Mladic's alleged lack of control over the VRS or his benevolent view of non-Serbs. As I will discuss, these claims are false. Indeed, when their basis is more closely examined, the evidence demonstrates the existence of the common purpose and General Mladic's many contributions to it. So I begin with some of the more extraordinary claims in the Defence's final brief. Faced with a massive trial record revealing the enormity of his crimes, crimes that he committed by using his authority to control the entire army, the Defence attempts to transform General Mladic into a benign but ineffectual officer, determined to protect Muslims against people like Karadzic, but unfortunately only a marginalised secondary figure, less important than the corps commanders. The fundamental principle that a general can delegate authority but not responsibility is turned on its head, as General Mladic now tries to pass off his responsibility for what he once bragged about by blaming his superior and his subordinates in an effort to exculpate himself. The Defence claims that command and control principles in the VRS meant that General Mladic could issue general instructions but was thereafter relegated to an advisory role because "exclusive" [Realtime transcript read in error "conclusive"] command was assumed by the corps commanders, whom they want you to believe were the most powerful and important people in the VRS. That's paragraphs 643 through 644 of the Defence brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I just check with you. The draft, at least the draft, reads "conclusive." Did I hear you say "exclusive"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, "exclusive." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thus, according to the Defence, Dragomir Milosevic and Galic were the ones who really controlled the army in Sarajevo. In Srebrenica - although the accused was physically present - command lay in the hands of Krstic. Para 644 of the Defence brief. That claim distorts the operative language by taking it out of context. For example, the Defence pretends that the term "exclusive" command in reference to a corps commander means that no one else can tell him what to do. In fact, the term means that within the corps, it is the commander who is at the top and no one else. At the same time, however, military doctrine and VRS regulations covering corps commanders recognise the existence of superior command. Indeed the Defence's conception of command would render the very concept of chain of command - with which have all become familiar during the course of this case - meaningless. It is not only facially preposterous, but it is belied by the extensive evidence you have heard from VRS and international witnesses that the chain of command was the operative principle. And in that chain, General Mladic carried out, fully carried out, his role as commander, issuing and overseeing the implementation of his orders to the corps commanders on a continuing basis. As General Milovanovic explained to you, the corps commanders would send the Main Staff in their daily reports, their decisions and plans for the following day's activities, which General Mladic would then approve or reject. That's T1696 through 97. But let's watch just half a minute from the war, 30 seconds which embody what the evidence has repeatedly shown about General Mladic's commanding role and which reflects the very absurdity of casting him as a secondary and marginal figure, as a mere advisor. Your Honours, this is the third Hotel Fontana meeting. The Chamber will recall General Mladic's domineering presence in each of the three meetings although one could be excused for forgetting the presence of other officers in the face of that dominance. Here, with Krstic sitting quietly by his side, this clip is a reminder of who was in charge, of who called the shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is General Mladic who makes clear what will happen to "your husbands, your brothers, your neighbours." This is just 30 seconds from a particular event, Your Honours, but it captures what has been proven over and over in intercepts, in written orders, in testimony about General Mladic's commanding presence and commanding role over the army. As you will hear in more detail from subsequent presentations, witnesses from virtually every level of command made clear that in the VRS you follow orders that come from the top and that move down the chain of command and that General Mladic was a superior commander over each of the corps commanders. And you can find that in the Prosecution final brief at paragraphs 94 through 109, 121 through 152, 253 through 271, 714 through 759. One of those witnesses put this reality in simple, concrete terms. When asked about the principles of unity of command and singleness of command, he said: "There's a pyramid. On the top of this pyramid is the Supreme Commander, the Chief of General Staff, and then it goes all the way down to the level of corporal and private. Everyone has their own superior and the superior has the right to issue orders and to supervise the implementation of those orders and those who are subordinates are in charge of carrying out those orders." That's found at T 5018.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we have the name of the person being quoted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's confidential, Mr. President, so I quote it just by reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As Kralj said: "The Army of Republika Srpska operates on the principle of subordination. And orders of superior officers, especially General Mladic, his orders were strictly adhered to and carried out." That's T27436. And, as Milovanovic testified, General Mladic, as commander of the Main Staff, had the right to issue orders to anyone in the VRS. That's T16923. Now, not content with claiming that it is his subordinate officers who are responsible, not him, General Mladic also claims that he was marginalised by Radovan Karadzic, with whom Mladic allegedly disagreed on how to treat Muslims. Now let's set aside for the moment such evidence as the fact that, as Karadzic put it, he and Mladic "talked about things as brothers" and their aim was to "move together towards the same goal." Set aside the fact that although Milovanovic heard talk of a conflict between Mladic and Karadzic, "especially after the war," during the entire course of the war he "never" saw them quarrel. That's T17107. But apart from these matters, according to the Defence, the "best illustration" of Mladic's claim is Directive 7. The Defence asserts that Karadzic bypassed General Mladic by sending Directive 7 directly on to the corps and that when General Mladic found out, he issued a superseding directive, Directive 7.1, that omitted the illegal order to create "an unbearable situation of total insecurity," to force Muslim civilians out. That's found at paragraphs 571 through 72 of the Defence brief. Directive 7 and 7/1 together, the Defence claims, "shows the disparity" between the criminally minded Karadzic, who wanted to illegally put pressure on the civilian population, and General Mladic who "took it upon himself" not to do that. That's at paragraphs 572 through 573. Now that is an epic story of moral bravery, and it is as false as it is dramatic. It rests on General Milovanovic's testimony that, A, Karadzic improperly sent Directive 7 directly to the corps, that's T16993 and 995; and that General Mladic omitted the illegal order from his directive to protect the civilian population, that's at transcript 16996. What the evidence actually reveals, however - what General Milovanovic was forced to admit when confronted with documents - is that Milovanovic forwarded Directive 7 to all the corps, not just to the 1 KK which he initially was forced to admit, but also to the Drina Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the Herzegovina Corps, all of which also belie General Milovanovic's preposterous claim that he saw the directive for the first time long after the war. That's at transcript 16996 through 99. As for the claim that the omission of the illegal order to make life unbearable reflected General Mladic's effort to protect civilians, that was exposed as false when Milovanovic admitted that details were omitted from 7/1 because they were "already contained in Directive 7," and that, in fact, Directive 7 remained operative. That's transcript 17126 through 27. And that is further in confirmed by the fact that in Directive 7/1 itself, General Mladic twice references Directive 7 as authority: On the basis of Directive number 7 -- or "in accordance with Directive number 7." That's P1470, page 2 and page 4. Beyond that, Directive 7 bears General Mladic's mark, echoing his intentions and indeed his words. As mentioned, Mladic's July 1994 meeting at the corps command was reflected in a Bratunac brigade information report which said: "The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." That's P1505, page 3, "unbearable." And on 8 March 1995, the day Karadzic signed Directive 7, General Mladic held a meeting at the Main Staff which was reflected in General Zivanovic's notebooks as "make life impossible." That's P5274, page 27. And you can find a detailed discussion at the Prosecution brief at paragraphs 426 through 452. This is just one of many examples, Your Honours, a portion of which you'll hear about over the next few days, of claims made in the Defence brief that crumble upon scrutiny. In contrast to the depiction of Karadzic, Mladic is cast as a beneficent protector of Muslims. Now, that is grounded on scattered examples, none of which supports the proposition such as the alleged protection of Muslim villages at paragraphs 685 through 690 of the Defence brief; the protection of Bosnian Croat civilians, 696 through 699; or that he issued orders or made pronouncements to protect civilians and obey international humanitarian law, for example, paragraphs 795 through 796, paragraph 414 of the Defence final brief. These references, however, do not support these assertions which in any event, Your Honours, are belied by the vast volume of evidence demonstrating General Mladic's commitment to the contrary. For example, Mladic's alleged protection of Bosnian Croat civilians is addressed at paragraph 459 of our brief, and that outlines the evidence demonstrating that this transfer was not altruistic, but arranged in order to advance Bosnia's division, to obtain military advantage for the Bosnian Serbs, for public relations purposes, and indeed for money. Similarly the claim that the Main Staff protected non-Serb villages relies on the testimony of General Sokanovic, that life in Muslim Podzeplje near the Main Staff continued unhindered. That claim is belied by the evidence that Podzeplje was burned to the ground in August 1992 following threats by Salapura to set on fire all Muslim villages in the area up to the Drina. That's at P3306, paragraphs 7 through 8. And also found at the Prosecution final brief at paragraph 305. As for orders to protect civilians and the alleged protection of Muslim villages -- Muslim and Croat victims, you will hear in subsequent presentations about the superficially cosmetic nature of General Mladic's toothless orders to obey international humanitarian law; and also about the cover-ups, systemic failures to prosecute, promotions and praise for perpetrators of those crimes - which more accurately reflected General Mladic's position on crimes against Muslims and Croats which fell within the common purpose. For that see Prosecution final brief paragraphs 490 through 491. And you will also hear, Your Honours, about how non-Serbs were treated, treated in the municipalities, in Sarajevo and in Srebrenica. And I will address you a bit later on the claim related to paragraph 414 of the Defence final brief and the 16th Session. More generally, the broad claim that General Mladic was a benefactor and protector of Muslims and Croats whose only ethnic distinctions were made for benevolent purposes simply cannot withstand the totality of the evidence. One candid moment caught on video of General Mladic on a short trip with a Serbian-Canadian supporter of the RS encapsulates what we have all learned and what the evidence shows about General Mladic's view of Muslims. Now that clip begins, you may recall, Your Honours, shortly after General Mladic has just explained that: "... whenever I come by Sarajevo, I kill someone in passing ... I go kick the hell out of the Turks. Who gives a fuck for them?" And now let's watch a short clip from the rest of that video.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Look what a house this Turkish motherfucker had." Showing off destroyed Muslim villages, Mladic exhibits pride and deep satisfaction at what he and his forces had achieved and nothing but contempt for the victims. These attitudes were also reflected in Mladic's conversation with Van Duijn, during which he crudely mimicked Muslims and told Van Duijn that the presence of a Nigerian in Van Duijn's unit was an indication that Mladic would be obliged to come to Holland in ten years to protect the Dutch from other races and from Muslims. You can find that at the Prosecution final brief paragraph 1201. The brazenly false attempt to depict himself as a Muslim benefactor and to blame his superior and his subordinates merely exposes General Mladic's awareness of the criminal nature of the plan to which he once boasted about contributing. That plan - which was formed before General Mladic was recruited to join - had its roots in events that took place before he returned to his birth republic in 1992, and that background will take us to some of the other Defence claims about the common purpose. In 1990, national elections were held in Bosnia in the wake of Communism's declining hold on political power. The three nationalist parties were overwhelming winners, essentially corresponding to their demographic ratio in Bosnia. Elated by the fall of Communism and what they saw as the re-awakening of Serbian consciousness, Bosnian Serb leaders nevertheless were concerned about the increasing risk of Yugoslavia's dissolution and the prospect that Bosnia would become a sovereign and independent nation. Even before the election, the SDS leadership expressed its categorical opposition to the possibility of Bosnia becoming sovereign and independent. As Karadzic said in an interview in July 1990: "The Serbs will not allow to live in some new NDH nor in some state which is without their matrix, Serbia." That's P7759, page 6. In the summer and fall of 1991, the SDS strongly supported JNA efforts in response to Croatia's independence and meanwhile attempted unsuccessfully to reach a negotiated solution with Muslims and Croats that would keep Bosnia in Yugoslavia, such as the Belgrade Initiative or the so-called historic agreement. In the face of the unsuccessful negotiations, however, by September 1991 the SDS had established several Serbian autonomous regions, the purpose of which was to "destroy" the unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's P7000 page 4 and page 6. When the Bosnian Muslims and Croats approved a memorandum of independence at the controversial 8th Session of the joint parliament on the 14th and 15th of October 1991, the Bosnian Serb leadership - in Karadzic's words to Milosevic - decided to "move on." As detailed in paragraphs 175 through 190 of the Prosecution brief, they established parallel institutions aimed at the creation of a Bosnian Serb state and organised the means to do so by force, if necessary. At the republic level, a parallel Bosnian Serb Assembly and a shadow government, the Council of Ministers, were established. At the municipal level, Karadzic issued instructions - the Variant A and B instructions - for the creation of Bosnian Serb Crisis Staffs that would spear-head the eventual take-over of the claimed areas. Karadzic began to emphasise during this period - as he would continue to do throughout the conflict - that Muslims and Croats were historical enemies whose inherent incompatibility with Serbs precluded co-existence. You find that at paragraphs 161 through 163 of the Prosecution brief. "Muslims and Serbs," he claimed, "were like a dog and a cat" or "plants that cannot grow side by side." See the Prosecution final brief footnote 603. Karadzic stressed the alleged demographic threat resulting from the Muslim birth-rate, his words casting them as an unstoppable demographic threat. "They'll overwhelm you with their birth-rate and tricks." That's P3900, page 36. Thus, even a minority of Muslims were a threat, much less the majority communities in eastern or north-west Bosnia ultimately claimed by the Bosnian Serbs. As Karadzic would tell the Assembly, explaining why smaller but ethnically pure territories were preferable to controlling all of Bosnia, with the Muslims the "23 per cent would rise to 24 per cent the day after, and the day after that one, it would be 25 per cent, because that is how it is with them." P3076, page 23 and 25. At the same time, however, the Bosnian Serb leadership claimed vast territories where Serbs and non-Serbs were intermingled, indeed where non-Serbs were the majority. Now, they attempted to justify these claims in various ways. For example, that Serbs were entitled to territory where they had been a majority before World War II; or that the plebiscite meant entitlement to any territory where a majority of Serbs - no matter how small a percentage of the actual population - had voted to stay in Yugoslavia; or justified simply on the basis that the area was deemed strategically significant to the Bosnian Serbs. You'll find that at paragraphs 1644 through 66. As Karadzic reminisced in 1995: "To tell the truth, there are towns that we've grabbed for ourselves and there were only 30 per cent of us. I can name as many of those as you want, but we cannot give up the towns where we made up 70 per cent. Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us there were in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica, in Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance, they had to become ours and no one is practically questioning it anymore." That's P4584, pages 17 through 18. As one witness observed, these undesired people on desired territory weren't going to disappear by magic. And separating them "is what ethnic cleansing was designed to do." That's P3103, transcript 4205. By late March 1992, as Bosnian independence loomed, Karadzic advised his officials that they could be confident that the number of Bosnian Serb police was sufficient and that soon the Bosnian Serbs would "literally assume control of the entire territory" of their municipalities, citing Zvornik as one example. That's P406, page 22. The take-over the Bijeljina a week later signalled the commencement of that process, sometimes accompanied by attacks on non-Serb villages and forcible removal of non-Serbs, sometimes by more slowly escalating forms of persecution. Serb authorities, including Slobodan Milosevic, helped implement the beginnings of the ethnic cleansing campaign through the JNA and the "strong support" the Bosnian Serbs had received from the DB, from State Security. That's P353, page 133. This included the deployment of Arkan's Men to Bijeljina and Zvornik. As Bell reported contemporaneously, Serb forces, including Arkan's Men, were "redrawing" the "ethnic map of Bosnia." That's P1874 and P832, page [sic] 24. Thus, by the time that General Mladic assumed command of the newly formed Army of Republika Srpska, the process of removing Muslims and Croats through a variety of crimes was under way, as he was duly informed. That's paragraphs 200 through 203. Indeed, by 12 May - when he was formally appointed Chief of the Main Staff - the nature of the cleansing campaign was obvious to the world. As the UN Secretary-General reported that day: "All international observers agree that what is happening is a concerted effort by the Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the acquiescence of and at least some support from the JNA, to create ethnically pure regions ... the techniques used are the seizure of territory by military force and intimidation of the non-Serb population." That's at P2814, paragraph 5. And when we return from our break, Your Honours, I would like to pick up on some of the Defence claims in respect of this evidence.

utterances.text: Yes, then all the technical problems apparently have been resolved. Mr. Mladic receives interpretation. Then we'll re-start and I'll repeat my first words. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. As I mentioned before we recessed, I had addressed some of the backdrop and development of the joint criminal enterprise which General Mladic joined in May of 1992. Now, in its brief, the Defence picks unsuccessfully at various aspects of this reality. And a closer examination of those claims will reveal - rather than disprove - the existence of the common purpose, and I'd like to take some of those at this point. The Defence argues, for example, that there is no evidence that anyone from the republic level "enforced" Variant A and B or monitored compliance with it. That's found at paragraph 462 of the Defence brief. Contrary to that claim, however, immediately after Variant A and B was issued, Karadzic assigned an emissary - Cizmovic - to "visit all our municipalities" to implement the Variant A and B papers that had just been issued. That's P4112, pages 2 and 3; and P2672, pages 3 through 4. And accordingly, on the 16th of January 1992, Cizmovic advised Karadzic that Bijeljina was "prepared for full co-operation with the instructions." That's P4115. And on the 22nd of January from a Krajina municipality, Cizmovic advised that things were "working," that a Crisis Staff would be created that night because "the objective must be carried out, instructions must be carried out." And that Cizmovic would be seeing about Birac, Romanija, and Herzegovina in due course. P6971, page 7. At the Assembly session on the 26th of January, 1992, Cizmovic called for the Variant A and B instructions to be carried out. That's P379, page 12. And on the 14th of February, Karadzic activated the second level of Variant A and B, telling a large extended group of his officials to introduce the "second level" and to intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and on every single millimetre of our territory." That's P3774, page 24. As Karadzic reminisced in 1995: "At the moment the war began, in the municipalities where we were the majority, we had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything. In the municipalities where we were in the minority, we set up secret government, Municipal Boards, Municipal Assemblies, presidents of Executive Boards. You will remember the A and B Variants." That's P4583, page 323. So - contrary to the Defence claim - there is not only some evidence but overwhelming evidence that Variant A and B was part of the plan. This is another of the many examples of assertions in the Defence final brief that are ostensibly demonstrated by evidence that does not, in fact, support the claim, or grounded on an assertion by a witness who revealed his lack of credibility or reliability, or indeed by a witness who recanted the point on cross-examination, or claims that are simply contradicted by the totality of the evidence. Now by way of another example, let's take Prijedor Crisis Staff member Mandic. Now, he's the Defence witness whose statement is cited more times than any other in relation to the overarching JCE, 42 times, and his statement is the sole support, for example, for propositions such as the Muslims in Hambarine put up a "strong resistance." That's at paragraph 930, footnote 2085 of the Defence brief. Or that people were released from Omarska when evidence showed that they had not broken the law. That's at paragraph 960, footnote 2158 of the Defence brief. Those assertions ignore the witness's acknowledgment in cross-examination that he no basis to make those claims, in fact, had contrary information; and you can find that at T28902 and 28909 through 910. And beyond those specific examples, this witness attested, under oath, to the accuracy of portions of his statement that he had recanted or qualified when he testified in Karadzic, under oath, prompting the Chamber to ask him to consider his attestation over a break. That's T28916 through 27. And beyond all that are the multiple contradictions that emerge when his claims are weighed against the totality of the evidence in this case. More generally, Your Honours, section 8 of the Prosecution final brief, beginning at page 689, discusses in detail witness credibility and evaluation of evidence. Over the course of the following days, we will continue to look beneath many of the Defence claims, exposing similar examples of assertions that are contradicted by a closer look of the evidence ostensibly supporting them and by the totality of evidence related to that point. But returning now to some of those claims in relation to the overarching JCE, the Defence also claims that the Crisis Staffs, led by local personalities who were allegedly focussed on only local interests, had "tremendous autonomy." That's found at paragraph 464 of the Defence brief. Now, this claim, too, unravels on examination. The claim that Crisis Staffs were autonomous is based on the testimony of Trifka Komad, a witness who told you under oath that Serbian -- that SAO did not mean Serbian Autonomous Regions, but claimed instead that the "S" stood for "independent." And he claimed that the Serb and non-Serb ballots for the November 1991 plebiscite had the same wording and that the differing colours were merely the result of a technical issue. Propositions so manifestly untrue that the Defence stipulated that - contrary to what he had said - it was Serbian Autonomous Regions and withdrew reliance on his testimony about the plebiscite ballot. That's found at transcript 28131 through 33. The examples of municipalities where the allegedly outsized personalities and narrow focus of local leaders supposedly distanced them from any republic-level plan are Rasula from Sanski Most and Stanic from Foca. Yet, in Sanski Most the Crisis Staff assigned its deputy president to be responsible for implementing "the ideas of the SDS leadership at the level of the republic, region, and municipality." That's P404, page 1. And in Foca, Crisis Staff President Stanic was forthright that: "We, the Serbs living to the west of the Drina river, know very well that our leaders are Dr. Radovan Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic." That's P7753. And Stanic's Crisis Staff informed Karadzic shortly before the conflict that: "We are ready to carry out any order you order." P3957. Once again, tug at the citation and it unravels, revealing a reality - instead - consistent with the Prosecution case. Now, the Defence also asserts that "some" Crisis Staffs displayed concern for how non-Serbs were treated, citing as two of its primary examples Sanski Most and the ARK Crisis Staff. That's at Defence brief paragraphs 450 through 451. Sanski Most. That's where the SDS newspaper the "Informator" informed Serbs that in pursuit of the "goal of creating a Serbian state," the SDS had organised and prepared Serbs for the "Bitter battle with the other two peoples, the Muslims if indeed are a people (they are not) and the Croats, who have forever carried in their genes a sick, a pathological desire and urge to kill those better, more honest and - do we need to say this? - stronger than they are." And the "Informator" continued that Serbs had finally abandoned the mistaken view that those people were anything other than "bloodthirsty villains who have never stopped in their religiously inspired drive to go for the blood of Serbhood." That's P705, page 6. Sanski Most, where the Crisis Staff concluded that captured civilians were to be used for exchange and where the VRS brutally cleansed Muslim villages in pretextual disarming operations after threats were issued to non-Serbs to "destroy and devastate your villages." That's P3302, page 7. Another prime example of alleged concern for Muslims by Crisis Staff was the ARK Crisis Staff which was headed by - indeed personified by - Radislav Brdjanin, whose philosophy was, as we learned, obedience to Karadzic above him and obedience from those beneath him in the hierarchy. That's P6997 and transcript T29759. Radislav Brdjanin, who relayed the orders from Karadzic to form the ARK Crisis Staff. That's T33986 through 87. And whose shared goals with Karadzic brought him to that position. P7757, page 7, and T34040 through 41. This leader whose "horns," as one witness put it, could have been "shortened" by Karadzic at any time. That's P6994, page 11; and T29785 through 86. This leader repeatedly called for Muslims to leave Banja Luka, stating that only a small percentage of Muslims could remain. That's P3989, pages 1 through 2; and P6994, page 8. Told a huge rally on the same podium with Karadzic that it was the obligation of Serbs to wipe their feet from the "foul non-Christians" befouling their soil. Page 6976, page 2. And who praised Omarska as "a job well done." P3959. Scratch the surface and the evidence exposes as false the suggestion that the ARK Crisis Staff was a kindly force, whose benevolent view of Muslims contradicts the common purpose. Now this failed attempt to depict Crisis Staffs as belying the common purpose is echoed by Defence efforts to suggest that other organs similarly reflected an absence of indications of the common purpose. Thus, in their discussion of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, the Defence cites the testimony of one of the Assembly's former members that he was not aware of a common plan to permanently remove other ethnicities. That's at paragraph 348 of the Defence brief. Now, that former member, Dodik, denied indeed that he had ever heard at Assembly sessions any indications, any hints of an intention, of a goal, or a process of moving or expelling Muslims. That's at T42299. That denial, however, did not square with the reality of what was said at various Assembly sessions. For example, the president of the SDS Executive Board and the co-ordinator of the Birac SAO, Rajko Dukic, talking about Eastern Bosnia in July 1992 said: "If we move further, there is Birac which is 100 to 108 kilometres away and has 120.000 Muslims. That is how many there were, but I hope that has at least been halved." P4581, page 73; see also P7082 and P7081, page 3, item number 4. Or these remarks at an Assembly session expressing concern that the language of a proposed law on citizenship suggests that: "The citizenship of Republika Srpska shall be acquired, among other things, by birth in the territory of Republika Srpska. This refers to all the Muslims and Croats we expelled; in reality they are citizens of Republika Srpska." That's P7196, page 10. And by the way, Your Honours, the bill was sent back for "improvement." And that's at P7196, page 11. Or this forthright acknowledgment of the goal of ethnic homogeneity and the resulting need for relocation: "Gentlemen, there is no Serbian state in Bosnian pot without gradual depopulation and relocating. If we want ethnically pure Serbian state - and we do, don't we? - if we all know and emphasise that we cannot live with them, then we have to realise that these draft maps are offering exactly that and that there has to be relocation." P2508, page 27. Or another statement in an Assembly session, expressing the concern that a proposed peace plan would mean that "everyone will be able to go back to their own territory," and "we will have to compensate everything we destroyed and burned and 17 mosques that we flattened" in that particular representative's municipality. That's P2508, page 22. Or any of the other similar Assembly references found in the final brief or to which we will be referring today. Again, when we peel back the assertion and examine the evidence on which it purportedly relies as well as the totality of the evidence that bears on that issue, the evidence reveals the common purpose. The Defence has also attempted to paint a picture of a Bosnian Serbs leadership whose passivity belies the existence or possibility of any common plan. They claim that the Bosnian Serbs were not preparing for war. Indeed "did not foresee war as a possible outcome," as evidenced by the "reactive decisions" made by the SDS. And that's at paragraph 312 of the Defence brief. These claims, first, founder on the evidence of Karadzic's repeated position that he and the SDS leadership knew far in advance the steps that they wanted to implement but waited for a politically expedient moment to do so. For example, Karadzic told members of the SFRY Presidency in December 1991: "We have made a list of moves, but we don't do anything -- we won't do anything until Alija messes something up. When Alija messes something up, we will make move number 5 and then we wait. When Alija messes something else up, we make move number 6." P4927, page 4. Or as he explained to the RS Assembly in 1994, there were nine to ten actions that the leadership had brain-stormed and then carried out. "Not all nine moves straight away" but "after Alija made a mistake." And that these pre-planned moves included the Serbian Autonomous Regions. That's P7762, pages 2 through 3. And in January 1995, Karadzic explained that his pre-planned steps included not only the regions, but bodies such as the Assembly. "We had a list of the actions and steps to take, but we always waited for the Muslims to make a mistake; and after they made one, we created a union of municipalities and the Serbian Autonomous areas next, followed by the regions, and eventually our Assembly and finally republic." P6999, page 3. Karadzic made clear to his officials as events were unfolding that "we have all the moves in the envelopes" and "we have plans for everything." That's D857, pages 6 through 7. He instructed them to conform to that time-table, advising SDS operative Stevandic to tell Brdjanin and Kupresanin "not to do anything stupid. We'll do everything Vojo and Brdjo think, but after the failure of the agreements that Alija will bring about. We'll accuse Alija for this failure." P7763. And make no mistake, those plans included territory. Babic recalled Karadzic and Jovica Stanisic long before the war clandestinely poring over maps of Bosnia with municipalities depicted in differing colours. That's P4166, T3406 through 08. Karadzic reminisced to the Assembly in 1994 about "making plans" before the war. "We were thinking then," he explained, about capturing certain features "so that the distance between Sarajevo and Banja Luka could be covered on a good road in 1.5. That is a state. That is a well-integrated nation. That was our plan back before the war." D639, page 9. But what about the Defence's claim that the Bosnian Serbs "did not foresee war as a possible outcome." That's again paragraph 312. Now, that claim would come, for example, as a great surprise to Cyrus Vance and Ambassador Okun, to whom Karadzic stated that if the Bosnian Serbs don't get what they want, they would get it through war. That's P3103, T4164, and pages 38 and 39. It would come as a surprise to Gojko Djogo, to whom Karadzic said that the Muslims would "disappear if there was a war. It will be a real bloodbath," Karadzic said. And he continued: "It will be said to Europe: 'Go fuck yourselves and do not come back before we finish the job.'" P4109, page 3, page 9, and page 24. The claim that the Bosnian Serb leadership did not foresee the possibility of war would come as a surprise to the Muslim and Croat members of the Joint Assembly, who Karadzic threatened in October 1991 that their moves toward independence would result in "the same highway of hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia went through. Don't think you won't take Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell and the Muslim people in possible extinction, because the Muslim people will not be able to defend itself if it comes to war here." P2004, page 3. And the claim that the Bosnian Serb leadership did not foresee war as a possibility would come as a surprise to Momcilo Krajisnik, who told the Assembly in February 1992: "We have two options: To fight by political means or to break off talks and go for what we have done over the centuries: Win our territories by force ... you know what our profession has always been: To wage war." P7005, pages 11 and 18. Momcilo Krajisnik, to whom Karadzic angrily said in January, talking about Izetbegovic: "Now he's talking openly of a sovereign and independent Bosnia. Does he want someone to destroy Sarajevo ... fuck him. We will release our Tigers and let them do their job." P2676, page 5. And the claim that the Bosnian Serb leadership did not foresee war as a possible outcome would come as a surprise to General Kukanjac, Mladic predecessor as head of the 2nd Military District, who reported in March 1992 that "the Serbian leadership and the Serbian people are fully prepared to wage war should the confederal option not be accepted." And that the SDS leadership in the Serbian population have "embraced the army," including that the JNA had "distributed 51.900 weapons (75 per cent) and the SDS 17.298" to Bosnian Serbs in various municipalities. That's P3030, pages 4 through 6. In short, contrary to the Defence claim, the Bosnian Serbs unmistakably "foresaw" the possibility of war, prepared for it, and indeed used the threat of their military and their military force to pressure their political opponents into abandoning moves toward independence. Once again, scratch the surface of the Defence brief, and it is the common purpose instead which is revealed. The Defence also claims that the Bosnian Serbs' involvement in negotiations - and that's found at paragraphs 292, 293, 298, 360 through 368 of the Defence brief - and particularly their involvement in the Cutileiro discussions: "Contradicts the Prosecution's allegation of the overarching JCE." That's at paragraph 364 -- 374. Again, contrary to this claim, the Bosnian Serb participation in negotiations was wholly compatible with the common purpose. First, of course, the pursuit of a negotiated dissolution does not gain, say, the attempt to achieve maximum objectives by force if a comprise is not reached. But beyond that, the Bosnian Serbs were not engaged in the Cutileiro negotiations out of some Gandhi-esque commitment to peace, but because it was clear to them that it could be used to destroy the possibility of a unitary Bosnia and to secure an ethnically defined state. Contrary to the representations made to Cutileiro at the time, the Bosnian Serb leadership did not actually accept the fundamental terms of the Statement of Principles. Now, perhaps the single key principle within the Statement of Principles was that Bosnia would be a state. That's found at T42409. As Karadzic told the Assembly, however: "The first position in all Cutileiro's principles, if you remember, was that Bosnia was a state consisting of this and that, but it was always said that Bosnia was a state and we never accepted that." P7023, page 2. As Cutileiro himself acknowledged in this Court, Karadzic withheld this position from Cutileiro and instead feigned agreement with the Statement of Principles. T42410 through 11. Similarly, the Statement of Principles did not envision that the Bosnian Serb entity would unite with Serbia. That's T42411. The Bosnian Serb leadership's goal, however, was to have the Bosnian Serbs "become part of the Serbian empire." P7005, page 18. And as Cutileiro acknowledged, if this view had actually been expressed, they wouldn't have had agreement. P7005 and T42411 through 13. Furthermore, the maps were "totally unacceptable to the Bosnian Serb leadership. That's P4582, page 4. The Bosnian Serbs - as Karadzic later explained - weren't satisfied with Eastern Bosnia, with Sarajevo, with the Neretva River Valley, or with what he called the "green stain," meaning Muslim areas in north-west Bosnia. P7294. So in the face of such fundamental disagreement, why did the Bosnian Serbs indicate agreement? They did so because they considered that they had "pulled" the Muslims into accepting that there would be a division, that it "would be based on ethnicity." D639, page 7. As Karadzic explained, that was "fatal" for Izetbegovic and Bosnia, and a "grave mistake" by the international community. The Bosnian Serbs had "led them" to believe that the process would be successful, but at that instant "Bosnia was finished. That's P4582, page 4. And as for the unacceptable maps, well those would be taken care of in a different way. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership considered that they had achieved the "quality," that is, ethnic division, and the destruction of Bosnia. And so all that was left was "a question of quantity." That's P4580. So what, Karadzic explained, if Bosnia remained within the current borders. "What matters is that the ones within Bosnia and Herzegovina become as wide as possible." P7005, page 10. So provided they made their borders with Bosnia sufficiently wide, this would be as good as staying in Yugoslavia. "As the popular saying goes," Karadzic told his officials, "if kicked out the door, go back through the window. You will still be in the same place." That's P7005, page 10. And that would be determined by the principle of the factual or de facto situation. As Karadzic told his SDS officials at the Assembly on the very day that the agreement in principle was at least temporarily reached, the quantity "will happen according to the actual conditions which are up to you to create." And Krajisnik told the Assembly at the very same session: "... it would be good if we could do one thing for strategic reasons, if we could start implementing what we have agreed upon, the ethnic division on the ground." P4580, pages 44 and 13. And then once it became clear that Izetbegovic, who - like international negotiators such as Darwin and Carrington - had from the outset doubts about the feasibility of ethnic divisions in an ethnically intermixed republic - and that's at T42393 and P7770, pages 3 and 4 - once it became clear that he had backed away, the Bosnian Serbs in Cutileiro's own words "went brutally on the offensive." P771 and T42446 through 47. Went on the offensive and took by brutal force those areas denied them in the original Cutileiro map, such as Eastern Bosnia, Sarajevo, Neretva, and the green stain that Karadzic referred to in north-west Bosnia. Contrary to the claims of the Defence, again, following the trail of the evidence leads inexorably to the common purpose. But while that was purposefully obscured in the context of the negotiations, those aims were repeatedly exposed - exposed in the cruel logic of policies that claimed vast territories inhabited by people with whom it was ostensibly to live, exposed in the pattern of cleansing in municipality after municipality, and also exposed in what the Bosnian Serb leaders revealed to internationals, what they conveyed to their subordinates, and what they said to each other. It was "obvious," crystal clear, to UN sector commander Abdel-Razek that there was a consensus among the Serb leaders and military commanders regarding cleansing. Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Plavsic acknowledged their plan for removal of Muslims from Serb territories, and Karadzic and Mladic once told him: "Muslims will be transferred out of Serb territory because we can't live together." And told him if we "miss this chance, we will not have it again." That's P293, paragraph 33. The Bosnian Serb leaders also explained to UN Representative Harland that historical circumstances required the removal of very large numbers of Bosnian Muslims, particularly in Eastern Bosnia and were open and wanting non-Serbs out of their territories. That's P1, paragraphs 270 and 274. Similarly, it was apparent to Anthony Banbury from his repeated meetings with the Bosnian Serbs leadership that: "Ethnic cleansing was a policy of the Bosnian Serbs. They wanted only Serbs living on the territory they controlled." That's P874, paragraph 63. As Ambassador Okun explained it: The position of the Bosnian Serb leadership throughout the whole period was that the people had to be separated, that they could not live together. Even though the populations were thoroughly intermixed, the Bosnian Serb leadership position was that they had to be taken apart. And that," Okun explained, "is of course what ethnic cleansing was designed to do. The leadership told him that Republika Srpska was to be as homogeneous ethnically, that is, ethnically 'pure' was the word that was often used by the Bosnian Serbs, ethnically pure as it could be." P3103, page 4169. And all Bosnian Serbs leaders were very consistent in their position that physical separation was needed and that the communities could not live together. P3103, T4205 and 4220. The policy was exposed to and known to Serbian and Croatian Serb leaders. For example, in July 1991, in a meeting in Slobodan Milosevic's office, Karadzic insisted that Babic not move forward with a proposed Krajina unification because it would interfere with the Bosnian Serb plans to form a Bosnian Serb entity that included territories where Serbs were a minority. Karadzic explained that they would wait for Alija to make a wrong political move and then link up the Serb territories by expelling Muslims. That's P4167, T13054 through 56, and P4166, T3401 through 04. It was known in the municipalities where local leaders implemented it. As Ilidza Crisis Staff President Prstojevic acknowledged in July 1992 when Karadzic "visited us in Ilidza and encouraged us, the Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory and even extended their territory in some areas, driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been a majority." That's P4581, page 66. On the 30th of June, 1992, Mladic and Karadzic met in Zvornik with military and civilian authorities from Zvornik, Vlasenica, Srebrenica, Bratunac, and other local areas, at which Zvornik TO Commander Pavlovic bragged to Karadzic: "We were most active in evicting the Muslims." And Crisis Staff President Grujic reported: "We have successfully implemented the president's decision to settle Divic and Kozluk with our children." The policy found expression in the selection by local leaders of particular percentages of Muslims and Croats allowed to leave [sic]. In Sanski Most 2 per cent, in Bijeljina 2 per cent, 5 to 6 per cent in Kljuc, and in Banja Luka and the ARK generally a small percentage. And you can find those respectively at P365; T6771 through 73; at P1054, paragraphs 11, 31 through 32; adjudicated fact 750; transcript 2050 through 51; and P3989, pages 1 through 3; P6994, page 8. And local leaders also acknowledged the common plan without reference to particular percentages, for example, the Rogatica Crisis Staff president and brigade commander referred on one instance to running late with the cleansing. P309, paragraphs 90 through 91.

utterances.text: Mr. Tieger would you please look at page 36, line 18, whether that is -- I don't remember what I heard, but whether that is what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm looking two lines further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I'm looking at the other -- allowed to, Muslims and Croats allowed to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Thank you. I appreciate that. It should say "allowed to remain."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
