utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When this policy was not fulfilled, the Bosnian Serbs leadership followed up. In personal meetings, Karadzic admonished Banja Luka mayor, Predrag Radic, for not having expelled non-Serbs or destroyed mosques, in contrast to other municipalities. You find that at the Prosecution brief paragraph 284, footnotes 1145 through 46. That was confirmed by Defence witness Solaja who testified about the constant pressure Radic was under from people at the political top and criticism of him because mosques were not [sic] standing. You can find that at T32751 through 52. Mosques were still standing. I think I said "not standing." So the criticism of Radic was for the fact that mosques remained and had not been destroyed. The common purpose was also acknowledged by Karadzic at various times, including when he explained to the Assembly his concern earlier in the war that Muslims might agree to peace proposals. Now why concerned? Because "we had some unfinished tasks related to military actions. I just prayed to God that nothing would be accepted because we had some tasks to complete." And what were those military tasks? Well, in Doboj, he said the Muslims had been in the relative majority, but "nowadays, Doboj is almost 100 per cent Serbian. The people from mountains moved into town, and so on. Thus, we can consider ourselves as winners after occupying this land since the land is 100 per cent Serbian now." That's P3076, pages 23, 25, and 26. The policy was acknowledged during a January 1993 meeting of Bosnian Serb and Serbian leaders, including Mladic, Karadzic, and Milosevic. When Serbian Foreign Minister Jovanovic urged Mladic and Karadzic to pursue the objective of making Bosnian Serb territory "nationally homogeneous as soon as possible" by more subtle means than ethnic cleansing because the international community was looking to catch them at the ethnic cleansings. Jovanovic also warned that freedom of movement might lead to mixing of the populations with the result that "what had been gained would gradually erode." Karadzic assured him that national homogenisation had already happened "to a huge extent," citing with pride Zvornik where there was 50/50 of us and now "the number of inhabitants of Zvornik is the same, approximately 50.000, and they are all Serbs." That's P7746, pages 14 through 16. The adoption of more subtle and deniable forms of purifying the territories was reflected in the Bosnian Serb leadership's use of Vojkan, who cleansed Bijeljina of thousands of remaining Muslims in 1994, prompting international complaints and false promises by the Bosnian Serbs leadership to investigate. See P7699, page 2, paragraph 7. As Karadzic reminded Mladic and others at a session of the Supreme Command, having Muslims remain is "disastrous for us." Vojkan's cleansing, however, under the guise of a private agency, permitted the leadership deniability, by "turning a blind eye" they could further our policy of "separation of peoples, of cultures, of worlds, and no one can accuse us." That's P6723, pages 6 through 7. In the face of such overwhelming evidence, the Defence suggests that an alleged republic-level policy that all citizens would be allowed to return belies the existence of the common purpose to permanently remove, and that's found at paragraph 459 of the Defence brief. What would be the point, they argue, of forcibly removing people only to let them back in? Well, as it happens, it is that very logic that explains why the Bosnian Serb leadership repeatedly made clear that it would ensure against the return of those they had expelled. From the very outset, the Bosnian Serb leadership had banked on the establishment of a factual situation to their advantage. As Karadzic explained to a gathering of top Serbian and Bosnian Serb officials at a meeting of the SFRY Presidency in December 1991, Serbs had to prepare to press their case on not only a legal basis but on "the factual basis." That's P4927. In the immediate aftermath of the Joint Assembly session at which Karadzic warned Muslims that moves toward independence threatened their very existence, Karadzic explained to Milosevic that the Bosnian Serbs were "moving on" to establish a "de facto situation ..." on 65 per cent of Bosnia which the Muslims will break their teeth on. That's P2659, pages 1 and 7. In mid-February 1992 when Karadzic activated the second level of Variant A and B, he told his officials that "now it would be more important to gain the real situation, the factual situation on the ground," which would allow Serbs to say to negotiators that maybe the Muslims are right but the factual situation controls. That's P3774, page 5. And as noted a few moments ago, a month after that, shortly before the take-overs began, Karadzic told his SDS officials at the Assembly that the quantity of their state "will happen according to the actual conditions which are up to you to create." P4580, page 44 through 13. And General Mladic and the VRS continued to implement the policy of creating a new factual situation and using it to control the ultimate territorial resolution. As General Mladic said: "Whoever holds the territory also draws the maps," and it was "the people and its army" who had drawn those maps." P1974, page 5. And like Okun, UNPROFOR recognised that General Mladic wanted them to "authenticate the new lines of ethnic division." That's P2810, paragraph 2. Karadzic underscored to General Mladic in 1992 that "the European community will accept the factual state of affairs and that is why we should not make a single concession in military terms." P354, page 22. And General Mladic conveyed the importance of that policy to his troops, reminding his corps command in Directive 2: "We liberated the territories we considered ours and created conditions for political and military leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that they could perform all activities and negotiations regarding the future state of BiH from the position of the stronger one in this territory." That's D99, page 1. And that message was indeed heard after the 1 KK had conducted ethnic cleansing operations throughout the ARK. 1 KK Commander Talic noted to Mladic the importance of insisting on "the factual situation." That's P360, page 54. "We liberated the territories." That's the language from the Directive 2 that we saw a moment ago in the previous slide. The Defence defends the terms "liberated" as meaning only "fighting against aggression." And that's found at the Defence final brief at paragraph 704. A more accurate understanding of its meaning, however, may be gleaned from a 6 June 1992 meeting at which a Bratunac municipal leader reported to Karadzic and Mladic, among others, that: "There are no Muslims now in Bratunac municipality. It is a fully liberated town." That's P353, page 101. The success of VRS operations meant that General Mladic would be able to report that the de facto approach had been successfully implemented. It 1993, General Mladic expressed the Main Staff's appreciation that "our negotiating team have done everything to change the factual state into permanent ..." and reminded Karadzic - as I noted earlier - "Mr. President, you have started from the most favourable starting position in Geneva. You had the military result in your hands." That's again P2508, page 33. I think it's time for a break, Your Honour, and we can continue in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, indeed, Mr. Tieger. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before we recessed, I had been discussing the creation of the factual situation. We broke with General Mladic reporting his satisfaction and pride about having presented the military result and the factual situation to the negotiators. Having thus made the factual situation a key part of their strategy for creating the state and defining its territory, the Bosnian Serb leadership was not about to relinquish it once achieved; instead, maintaining the homogeneity or areas remained a keystone so that, as Jovanovic had urged, what had been gained would not be eroded. Now, you recall that the Bosnian Serb leadership acknowledged to Harland their pressure on the Bosnian government to accept the ethnic cleansing, the redistribution of the populations. That's P1, para 270. Ambassador Okun also recognised that the Bosnian Serbs were attempting to cement the cleansing, in contrast to undoing it, as the Defence claims, noting that "their whole claim, for example, for the Drina River Valley, that is to say for the left bank of the Drina, was based on ethnic cleansing. I mean, they knew it; we knew it." P3103, transcript 4192. Okun also recalled the Bosnian Serb leadership's call "to accommodate ethnic realities," which Okun explained was a "very clear, not so subtle" reference to ethnic cleansing. P3103, T4215 through 16. One transparent strategem for cementing the cleansing was their call for referendums in which the inhabitants of territory would vote on which entity they wished to be in. And as Okun explained: "Holding a referendum in areas that you've ethnically cleansed looks like a pretty good deal to the cleanser." And that's P3103, T4245. Karadzic made crystal clear to his officials that Bosnian Serb negotiators would insist that the allocation of territory in any peace process would be governed by the factual situation they had created, that is, by what the VRS had achieved. They would explain, for example, that while Zvornik was once 60/40 to the advantage of Muslims, as he said: "We request Zvornik based on the right which comes out of the new reality ... this war has created the new reality. There are now the Serbs from Zenica here. If you want to give Zvornik to the Muslims, then you have to wage a new war in order to expel these Serbs back to Zenica. We request Zvornik according to this right." P7357, page 5. May I ask the Court Officer, please, to display the -- thank you. Further, the Bosnian Serb leadership was equally clear that it would not allow the results of the ethnic cleansing to be undone by a right of return. So when a representative complained to Karadzic that a proposed peace agreement meant that "everyone will be able to go back to their own territory," Karadzic assured him that the Bosnian Serbs would control their borders and "we will have barbed wire for ten years." P2508, pages 22 through 23. And that was regardless of what they might have to promise the international community. So when Deputies Club President Maksimovic insisted that not even "500 or more Muslims" should be allowed back, that's P3076, page 36, Karadzic elucidated one of his ploys to frustrate international efforts to ensure return. He agreed that "what Mr. Maksimovic has said is correct," but explained that under international law, they would not be permitted to ban return. That is why, Karadzic noted, he had insisted on a "two-way process." That's P3076, page 38. And this meant - as he elaborated at a subsequent Assembly session - that "Muslims from Kozluk can return to Kozluk if the Serbs from Kozluk return to Zenica." And Serbs from Zvornik weren't going anywhere. As Karadzic explained: "We can act the Serbian Cyrillic way and tell it all to their face, or we can be a bit cunning. We do have to be a bit cunning." P4584, page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I urge you to here and there slow down a bit because sometimes part of what you are telling us are missing in the provisional transcripts, and we'd like to be able to read everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Will do. The Bosnian Serb leadership also established a demographic programme to resettle Serbian refugees into areas successfully targeted by the Strategic Objectives in order to cement the forcible displacement of non-Serbs. And see paragraphs 475 through 77 of the Prosecution brief. The objective of that programme was epitomised by its co-chair Radislav Brdjanin, a man devoted to homogenous territories. Brdjanin once defended a housing law against criticism that it might invite the return of Muslims by saying: "Gentlemen, you cannot fool me that you believe in the greatest wonder of the world, such as that Brdjanin could participate in a process of return of Croats and Muslims." That's P6742, page 11. Once again, peel back the Defence allegation - in this instance the claim that expelled refugees were "free to return," that's paragraph 459 of their brief; and the evidence exposes not only the inaccuracy of the claim but the existence of the common purpose. Now, as discussed to some extent earlier, the Defence attempts to paint General Mladic as a protector of Muslims and Croats. And in part, this rests on repeated claims throughout their brief that General Mladic's remarks at the Assembly session at which he was formally appointed Chief of the Main Staff reflect his protective and benevolent views toward non-Serbs, and that's found at various parts of the Defence brief, 559, 115, 568, 412 through 415, 788, and so on. Now, first it is surprising to find this speech cited in support of Mladic's alleged good intentions toward the non-Serbs, in view of such things as his criticism for simply "spitting" on Sarajevo with a few mortars, his call for it to be ringed with 300 mortars, his statement that he would make Sarajevo "even less" than useless to anyone, and his call to deprive it of utilities while blaming Muslims. That's found at Prosecution brief 617 through 623. But beyond that, taking the Defence citations in context and in light of the totality of evidence, the 16th Session including General Mladic's speech is, again, further corroboration of the common purpose. Now by the date of that session, May 12th, the existing Bosnian Serb forces and authorities had taken control of nearly all of the claimed territories -- the claimed municipalities at any rate. While non-Serbs have been forced out of some areas, the bulk of the cleansing to sufficiently homogenise those municipalities and those territories had not yet taken place. And during this period, while the seizures were taking place and before General Mladic's accession, Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership intensified efforts that had begun months earlier to create a Bosnian Serb army and, in particular, to find the right person to successfully lead that army and the implementation of Bosnian Serb goals. Unsurprisingly, Karadzic looked to events in Croatia where Serb forces had forcibly displaced ethnic Croats from Serb-claimed areas to create a Serbian state - for that see paragraphs 204 through 208 of the Prosecution brief - an effort that was strongly supported by the Bosnian Serb leadership. For example, P2668 and P2671. Indeed, Karadzic considered the RSK as an example and inspiration. That's P3978, page 11. And he used Croatia's fate as an example, that is, "the same highway of hell and suffering," when he warned the Bosnian parliament that an independence initiative would result in the possible extinction of the Muslim people. Again, that's P2004, page 3. And as detailed in paragraphs 204 through 208 of our brief, General Mladic was a key figure on that highway of hell. Upon arrival in Croatia, he changed the role of the JNA from one of buffer between the two sides to one of siding with the Serbs. That's P7638. And in that new capacity, General Mladic led attacks on towns and villages, including Kijevo, Drnis, Sibenik, Sinj, Srbinje, advancing Serbian territorial objectives through destruction of towns, killings, and expulsion of inhabitants. He used previous attacks as threats of what lay in store for others, for example, telling an interlocutor that "Kijevo will be a garden of flowers compared to what you will experience if you should touch me." His view of how to achieve his objectives was further captured in these comments: "Nothing will get out the of Dalmatia except children under the age of 10 if they carry on like this, all that is older than 10 and younger than 75 will come to harm in Sibenik and we will not leave a single house standing, unless they finish the job like it was done in Sinj." That's P1959, also P7052 which duplicates at page 8. Karadzic had heard of Mladic and "took an interest in him." P4583, page 324. He and Krajisnik went to General Kukanjac's office and listened to Mladic "issuing orders and commanding around Kupres and Knin." And thereafter, as he told the Assembly: "Gentlemen, we got the officers we asked for. I asked for Mladic." That's P4583, page 324. General Mladic, the man Karadzic once referred to as "the glorious fighter from Krajina." P2001, page 118. As discussed as paragraph 20 of the Prosecution brief. On April 30th, 1992, at a meeting with Milosevic and other Serbian and SFRY leaders, the Bosnian Serbs "got their own military," including the agreement that General Mladic would become commander of the soon-to-be Bosnian Serb army. Within days General Mladic was meeting with the Bosnian Serb leadership and others to formulate the strategic objectives that would guide the nascent army. And that's found at Prosecution brief, paragraph 209. Days later, at the 16th Session, Karadzic reported on political conditions and the war, in the course of which he enunciated the six Strategic Objectives. The achievement of all six goals, he said, would "finally finish the job of the freedom struggle of the Serbian people." That's P431, page 10. After Karadzic spoke, a number of officials took the floor and some of whom suggested that geographic areas not embraced by the objectives, for example, Tuzla and Bihac, should be included. Brdjanin, for example, on his part expressed dismay that a Muslim colonel was teaching political education for the Banja Luka Corps. "How can anyone still believe it is all right that we have a Muslim doing political education in the Banja Luka Corps?" That's at P431, pages 13, 23 and 25. And although General Mladic had not been on the agenda to speak at that point, he "asked for the floor" after listening to these remarks. That's at page 31 of P431. And he conveyed what would one would expect from a man who had been selected to lead the army on the basis of his Croatia credentials. "I know what I'm doing. Let's stick to the goals that the other leaders and I have come up and not make things harder for ourselves by trying to do too much or by revealing our secret plan." General Mladic immediately and repeatedly cited his experiences in Croatia as validation of his expertise and reflections of what he intended to do, including an anecdote about shelling a hotel housing European community monitors to enforce his demands, prompting response at the time: "Mladic are you sane?" P431, page 37. General Mladic explained: "We have only made our first move in the war." And that they had to be realistic and stated: "The goals that I've heard here and the demands, please, even if we had an army like the Chinese, it is doubtful that we could fulfil them." And then he explained: People are not simply keys in a pocket that can be shifted from here to there. "It is something easily said but difficult to achieve." P431 all of pages 32 to 34. And he reminded the Assembly that: "The thing that we are doing needs to be guarded as our deepest secret." Than their representatives needed to present their goals in a way that will sound appealing to the international community while at the same time "our people must know how to read between the lines." That's page 34 of that P431. And he also blasted Brdjanin for his criticism of the Muslim teaching within the Banja Luka Corps. "I know to whom it referred," General Mladic said. It refers to Colonel Hasotic. And he explained that it was better to have Hasotic who had served in Croatia and who "knows better how to neutralise me," with them than fighting against them. And so he explained: You can't have a sieve to get rid of everyone, that would include guys like Hasotic. And beyond that, how would that square with the concerns he had just expressed about appeasing the international community? How would Karadzic and Krajisnik explain that? And that's at page 35. And similarly he referred to his recent visit to Kalinovik, where frightened Muslim villagers "fear, might prays to no God" met with him in a scene which brought to mind - as Minister of Information Ostojic who was with him explained - a master-servant relationship. And that's found at P431, page 7. And so those cowed, subservient Muslims in General Mladic's Serbian majority hometown with whom he just met were, like Hasotic, among those who might not have to be explained to the international community and might not have to be expelled or drowned. That was the context of General Mladic's remarks. And thereafter, he oversaw - before the month was out - the beginning of the VRS's brutal implementation of the Strategic Objectives in Muslim and Croat villages, towns, and communities. As Defence expert Kovic acknowledged: One should look to what happened on the ground when determining what someone intended. And that's at T42007. The Defence, however, seeks to distance Mladic from the Strategic Objectives and to neutralise them. They claim, first, that the Strategic Objectives had nothing to do with the common plan to permanently remove, arguing that the Prosecution ignores that Karadzic defined the first goal as "separation of states." That's para 410. What the Defence fails to mention is that after mentioning states, Karadzic immediately went on to make clear that the separation was about people. "Separation from those who are our enemies and who have used every opportunity, especially in this century, to attack us and who would continue with such practices if we were to stay together in the same state." That's P431, page 9. General Mladic certainly knew what he meant. Only a few days before, on 6 May in one of their meetings about the Strategic Objectives, Karadzic had enthused: "We are on the threshold of achieving our centuries'-old dream of creating our own state without many internal enemies." That's P352, pages 257 through 258. Similarly General Gvero - also in attendance at the 16th Session - understood that: "Everybody has to live on his own territory, Muslim on Muslim territory, Serbs on Serbian." P7394, page 3. The Defence also claims that at the 16th Session: "There is a notable absence of discussions on separating or moving Muslims." That's found at paragraph 413 of their brief. This claim simply disregards such comments as Radic's on the process of "resettlement." Or Milojevic's references to the fact that the borders relating to the Strategic Objectives "intrinsically implies moving a contingent of the population," or the reference to the "happy news" that the Strategic Objectives meant that Muslims who had been relocated across the Una River would not be returning. And those are found at P431, pages 15, 33, and 20 respectively. The Defence further contends that while General Mladic may have heard of the Strategic Objectives he "provides no insight" into their formulation or implementation and the evidence does not support the claim that he formulated or implemented them. That's at paragraphs 419 through 20. Now this false claim ignores such evidence as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I again ask you to slow down a bit. It's not only transcription but also French translation, which easily is a few lines behind. So please slowly proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was addressing the Defence claim that the evidence doesn't support the assertion that he formulated - that is, General Mladic formulated or implemented the Strategic Objectives. This claim ignores such facts as the following: 1. That General Mladic expressly said at the 16th that: "I have read, mulled over for a long time and discussed within the most select circle of comrades whom we convened the strategic goals that are of substance." P431, page 32. 2. That Milovanovic said: "So far our army has achieved four strategic goals, that is, the tasks." Adding: "And that is the basis from which we embark on the negotiations." P7764, page 2. That Mladic told the Assembly: "The tasks in the army in this war stem from the known six Strategic Objectives adopted by our Assembly." P4583, page 22. Or that the combat-readiness report stated that the -- states that: "The Strategic Objectives served as the guide-lines for planning the actual operations and concerted battles." Page 338, page 159. Or just one more example, that at a meeting on the 8th of November, 1992, a meeting including General Mladic, Karadzic, Krajisnik, and corps commanders, a meeting that focussed on the importance of the Drina, Krajisnik noted that the army had achieved some of the Strategic Objectives but not all, including Strategic Objective number 3. Therefore, he said, the most important task was the mopping up - the "ciscenje" - of the Drina by the Drina Corps; and Directive 4, ordering the Drina Corps to force the Muslim population in the Podrinje to leave was issued two weeks later. That's P356, pages 146 through 147; and P976, page 5. Once again, Your Honours, scratch the surface and the common purpose is revealed. Now, I have mentioned throughout my remarks this morning and early this afternoon the disparity between the propositions made by the Defence and the citations supporting them. The caution required in considering those assertions extends to the legal propositions in the Defence brief. For example, the Defence proffers a sweeping but wholly uninformed attack on JCE liability, which is grounded throughout on a disregard for Appeals Chamber jurisprudence, claiming that Tadic -- the Tadic case should be limited to small-scale cases. They disregard Krajisnik at para 469, Brdjanin at paragraphs 422 through 425, and Djordjevic at para 40. Challenging whether JCE liability exists as a matter -- as a part of customary law, they disregard Djordjevic's confirmation at paragraphs 43 through 44 of the validity of the Tadic approach. In a similar manner, Popovic at paragraph 1674; and Djordjevic at para 50 and 52 make clear that findings of other courts outside the Tribunal are not binding. Sainovic para 611 and Kvocka at 115 through 119 hold that a common plan or design may be inferred from the facts and don't require proof of any additional agreement between the accused and other JCE members. Similarly, contrary to Defence arguments, Brdjanin at paragraphs 413 through 414 holds that a JCE member can be held accountable for acts of physical perpetration of non-JCE members. You can also see Stanisic/Zupljanin at paragraphs 994 through 96. The Defence claims that General Mladic is not responsible for crimes at detention facilities he allegedly did not control ignore the Martic judgement at paragraphs 187 through 89, 195, 215 and 210; and the Stanisic/Zupljanin judgement at paragraph 96 and Brdjanin at paragraph 410. Similarly, the Defence attempt to import new requirements for JCE 3 liability, have been rejected already by Stanisic/Zupljanin at paragraphs 963 through 966; and the Appeals Chamber has repeatedly affirmed the standards set out by the Prosecution, for example, Stanisic/Zupljanin at 595 and 614; Sainovic, 1061, 1557; Brdjanin, 365 and 411. And with respect to the fact that JCE liability applies to all crimes, including specific-intent crimes, see Stanisic/Zupljanin paragraph 599; the Brdjanin interlocutory appeal on the 19th of March, 2004; and Djordjevic at paragraph 919. These same mischaracterisations of law, coupled with misstatements of fact, are applied by the Defence to Count 11, hostages. So, for example, the Defence asserts in paragraphs 165 through 169 of its brief that Count 11 is "procedurally defective" because Common Article 3 lays down the minimum criterion that the parties must respect during an internal conflict and the conflict in BiH was international in 1995. Contrary to the Defence claim, the Tribunal has held, including in the context of hostage-taking, that Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions applies to both international and non-international armed conflicts. That's the Karadzic Trial Chamber, 28 April 2009, paragraph 59, referring to the Appeals Chamber decision in Tadic on the 2nd of October, 1995. You can also see Delalic on 20 February 2001 at paragraph 150. The Delalic Appeals Chamber, in fact, called it "legally and morally untenable" to interpret the protections under Common Article 3 as inapplicable to an international conflict. The Defence claim that Count 11 is procedurally defective is baseless and contrary to settled law. Similarly, the Defence asserts at paragraph 3313 of its brief that although certain courts have held that detained peacekeepers enjoy the protections of Common Article 3, the UN detainees in this case gave up such protection by actively participating in the conflict. Now, this claim chooses, first, to disregard the very language of Common Article 3, which expressly applies "to persons taking no active part in the hostilities including members of armed forces placed hors de combat by, inter alia, detention." It also ignores Tribunal jurisprudence confirming that the prohibition on hostage-taking is "absolute and without exception" and that it applies to UN personnel, irrespective of their status prior to detention. And for that, see the Karadzic Appeals Chamber 98 bis decision on 11 December 2012, paragraph 16. These mischaracterisations of law in respect of the hostage count are matched by Defence mischaracterisations of fact. They claim, for example, that around 28 May 1995, General Mladic had a conversation with Smith in which he was calm, threatened no one, and said that no threats had been made against detainees. That's at paragraph 3382. Now, apart from the fact that in that very conversation, General Mladic acknowledged that some of the detained personnel were held at potential targets for NATO - that's P2558 - this claim ignores such evidence as the following. First, it ignores General Mladic's conversation with Smith two days earlier, during which Mladic told Smith that if there were further air-strikes, UNMOs would be killed and that the fate of the hostages was in Smith's hands. That's P7540, page 2; and P2557 page 4; P791. It ignores that Kalabrcyk was handcuffed and filmed at the Jahorina radar site because Mladic wanted UN people filmed at that location. 2554, page 13. It ignores that General Milovanovic issued a Main Staff order - approved by the Supreme Commander - to distribute 103 detainees to various corps and deploy them at warehouses in the corps "in order to prevent NATO leaders from carrying out their intentions." And it ignores that on 30th of May, 1995, General Mladic ordered the SRK to "complete the disarming of the captured UNPROFOR members and their deployment to the facilities which have been assessed as possible NATO air-strike targets." That's P5230, paragraph 7, page 3. And one further legal matter, two additional legal matters. One, the Defence also asserts the Prosecution is required to prove that the physical perpetrators or the tools of the JCE possessed the specific intent required for genocide. That's at paragraph 251. The intent of the physical perpetrator, of course, is relevant only to the extent that the Trial Chamber could find that neither Mladic nor any member of the JCE had the requisite mens rea and genocidal intent. That's found at Krajisnik Appeals Judgement para 226; Brdjanin appeals judgement, para 410. And were that to happen in this instance, the Chamber would then consider, pursuant to JCE 3, the destructive intent of such persons as Drljaca or Zeljaja according to the elements of Article 4 that I will be discussing tomorrow. And finally, Mr. President, Your Honours, let me quickly address the 73 bis argument, another Defence claim that is frankly untethered to reality. The reduction pursuant to 73 bis in this case was clearly about Scheduled Incidents, as reflected in the very first paragraph of the Prosecution's submission. After explaining in paragraph 1 which of the "crimes enumerated in the schedules" it would present evidence on, it noted again in paragraph 7 that it had identified "the scheduled crimes" upon which it would present evidence and that it would not present evidence on the remainder of the previously scheduled crimes, resulting in a reduction of the case. Thereafter, the Trial Chamber adopted the proposal and ordered the Prosecution to file an amended indictment in accordance with the decision, which the Prosecution did. The Amended Indictment crossed out the identified Scheduled Incidents and - unsurprisingly - all the counts remained. No objection was made to this indictment with all 11 counts. Thereafter, the Prosecution led evidence on forcible transfer and deportation. No objections were made to that evidence on the basis of a claim that counts -- the counts related to forcible transfer and deportation had been dropped. At 98 bis, the Chamber found a case to answer on all 11 counts, and the Defence did not object that Counts 7 and 8 had been dropped. The Defence then called extensive evidence related to forcible transfer and deportation, and there is no evidence -- there is no suggestion that these were superfluous because the counts had been dropped. In short, the preposterous interpretation proffered now by the Defence is belied by the fact that no one interpreted the 73 bis decision in that patently unreasonable manner during the entire course of the subsequent five years. Mr. President, Your Honours, that concludes my presentation this morning. Mr. Traldi will now address aspects of the implementation of the overarching JCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. I take it that the stage has to be changed slightly. Mr. Traldi, since you were present, you certainly have heard my observations as to the speed of speech which I addressed to Mr. Tieger, but which equally apply to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At least equally, I'm sure, Your Honour. And I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Beginning immediately after the 16th Assembly, General Mladic led the ethnic cleansing campaign which implemented the common criminal purpose Mr. Tieger just described. In carrying out the cleansing campaign, his VRS and other Bosnian Serb forces committed a constant pattern of crimes throughout Serb-claimed territory, particularly in the charged municipalities. Mladic used his command and control over the VRS to lead this campaign. Indeed, he escalated the cleansing campaign immediately after the VRS began to function under its own name on 19 May 1992. In the first two weeks of its existence, the VRS led ethnic cleansing operations in six different indictment municipalities. These operations included eight of the massacres General Mladic is charged with; and during that same period, VRS units and other Bosnian Serb forces established camps at which they detained and abused non-Serb civilians at Manjaca, in Banja Luka; Susica, in Vlasenica; the Veljko Vlahovic school in Rogatica; and Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje in Prijedor. Mladic used his control of his subordinates to achieve the cleansing he had told the 16th Assembly would be difficult through a pattern of terrible crimes. In municipality after municipality, the cleansing campaign tore apart non-Serb families and communities and left behind destroyed mosques and Catholic churches, the burned-out and empty shells of Muslim and Croat villages, and mass graves full of victims, while many of those who had not been killed or fled huddled in terror in camps, waiting to see which detainees would be the next to be brutalised. I will first be discussing General Mladic's command and control, then his use of that command and control to operationalise the common purpose, and then his knowledge and approval of the cleansing campaign. And finally I'll address some issues related to several of the specific municipalities. The evidence shows what witnesses told you they saw from the beginning of the war: Mladic had firm command and control over the VRS and subordinated Bosnian Serb forces throughout this campaign. Brigade General Wilson, who was present in Bosnia from the establishment of the VRS, testified its operations were sophisticated, well-organised, requiring good command and control. And Colonel Tucker explained nothing of any military significance could happen in Republika Srpska without Mladic's specific approval: "It was very apparent that he made all the practical military decisions that mattered." At the 16th Assembly, Mladic made clear he insisted on single command, telling the Assembly: "I do how to command an army but to be able to command, I need to have an army, and we cannot have 100 masters in one home. The army must have a unified command." He took immediate measures to ensure that single command beginning, in fact, even before the 16th Assembly. The day afterwards, Ilidza Crisis Staff member Unkovic asked Mladic if Arkan's men in Ilidza were under Mladic's command, and this was Mladic's response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I do not hear anything on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I didn't either, Your Honour, and I'm told it's because I neglected to tell the booths that it's P403, which -- the transcript of which they have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... portion of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's a portion which has been identified in what we've given them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let's re-start if everyone is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] "U: One more question. "M: Yes. "U: We have some Arkan's Men here. "M: Yes. "U: Are they under our command? "M: All of them, all under arms are under my command if they want to stay alive."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: By this point, Mladic was already issuing orders, still formally on the letterhead of the JNA 2nd Military District and through its chain of command, like P3056 and 3057. As Milovanovic testified, then JNA corps were sending combat reports in to Main Staff headquarters and Mladic was on the phone exercising command, as you've just heard, and, for instance, over the Kalinovik Tactical Group in P1597. On 19 May, General Gvero informed subordinate VRS units that Mladic was the VRS's commander and: "All the other important elements of a united organisation and leadership and command have also been established." And that's P7325, page 2. So the Main Staff concluded it had effective control over Bosnian Serb military forces as of the 19th of May. The VRS inherited much of this command structure, including its personnel, weapons, and Mladic himself from the JNA. As we set out in our brief, paragraphs 11 to 32, this was the culmination of a plan to create a Bosnian Serb army, which the JCE members had shared beginning in December 1991 and which Slobodan Milosevic had initiated. And you'll see on the next two slides Borislav Jovic's notes of meetings with Milosevic, first reflecting his decision to transfer JNA personnel so that the Serb leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina could "assume command over the Serb part of the JNA." And Jovic's notes show soldiers were quickly redeployed consistent with this plan. And then, on 30th of April, 1992, the need to "withdraw the remainder of the soldiers who are FRY citizens from Bosnia-Herzegovina so that the remaining 90.000 JNA soldiers in that republic, mostly of Serb nationality, could be placed under the command of the Bosnian Serb leadership. And that's P3084, pages 29 to 32. Because of this plan and the preparations the JCE members made, Mladic took over a well-functioning army established to implement the common purpose. And the Defence argues the JNA in Bosnia was ill organised and a neutral force. Both arguments fail on close scrutiny. In fact, when Mladic took command, the JNA 2nd Military District was a well-functioning military that was part of the JCE in Bosnia. Under the control of JCE member Slobodan Milosevic, the JNA had worked in concert with the Bosnian Serb leadership to begin implementing the common purpose. We lay the evidence for that out in our brief, particularly in paragraphs 17 to 23, 193, and 546 to 547. And you see various JNA corps transform into VRS corps, for instance, in Defence witness Kelecevic's testimony at transcript page 37138; and in 4th Corps officer Gagovic's order, P6534. And the Defence attempts to deny even that the VRS acquired JNA weapons, but Mladic himself had stated during the war: "Our army is one of the rare ones in history to have started a liberation war with a very solid material base." P1966, page 5. And his predecessor as 2nd Military District Commander Kukanjac explained after the war: "The Muslim-Croat horde never got hold of a single plane, helicopter, tank, armoured personnel carrier, gun, mortar, or motor vehicle." And once the VRS was formed, Mladic had strong command and control. As Milovanovic explained: "Command is centralised first and foremost and it goes top to bottom from the Supreme Command across the Main Staff, corps commands, and down the chain to squads." That's at transcript page 16932. And he goes on to explain how the Main Staff monitored the implementation of its orders and the activities of corps commands. And General Wilson, among others, gave evidence that Mladic's effective control over VRS units was visible to him. And that's P320, paragraph 127. The combat-readiness report of the Main Staff explained that it had translated objectives and tasks set by the political leadership into "missions of the Army of RS, with the goals of every individual combat action, operation, or battle being specifically defined." It concluded decisions on the engagement of the forces of the VRS were taken at meetings of bodies of the Main Staff headed as a rule by the commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Traldi, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That is, by General Mladic. That's P338, page 8. And after the war, Mladic explained the most complicated and difficult decisions he often made alone or with his Chief of Staff. That's P1147, page 124. In paragraph 636 of its brief, the Defence suggests that the military police may have carried out tasks from the security organ without Mladic's knowledge, in an effort to separate him from the crimes the military police were committing, but the security organ was run by General Tolimir - one of Mladic's trusted subordinates from Croatia as can you see in P5007. Mladic described him as part of the inner core of the Main Staff. The presence of a lieutenant like Tolimir under Mladic's command and supervising the professional work of the military police supported Mladic's command and control over them, but Mladic was the one with command, as Skrbic explained. Mladic's various assistant commanders would make proposals to him in their areas of responsibility and if Mladic agreed, they were responsible for implementing those proposals. And Mladic kept firm control over even his most trusted subordinates. For instance, he made clear to Tolimir in May 1992 that Tolimir had on one occasion gone beyond his remit telling him: "Don't exceed your powers and competencies anymore." Amd Tolimir replied: "I understand, Comrade General." Mladic added: "And don't bow to pressure anymore." And Tolimir again replied: "I understand, Comrade General." The next day when Mandic notified Tolimir of an order from Mladic, Tolimir simply replied: "Well, that's clear." And that's P2752 and P2755. Mladic also exercised firm control over corps commanders. SRK commander Dragomir Milosevic was described by international as "merely adhering to the orders/directions that were issued to him by General Mladic. And Milosevic's assistant commander for legal, morale, and religious affairs, Luka Dragovic, testified that as far as he knew, Milosevic abided by Main Staff decisions and "never issued an order that was in contravention of orders from the superior command." As Mr. Tieger mentioned, corps commanders would seek approval for the next day's decisions in their daily reports, and you see that process illustrated, for instance, in P3663, P3672, P4045, and P4450. And East Bosnia Corps commander Simic testified he had the right to call Mladic urgently "to ask for approval of some of our decisions." And that's P4325, transcript page 28494. And corps commanders passed Mladic's orders down the chain to the units. Defence witness Milivoje Simic acknowledged 1st Krajina Corps Commander Talic's orders were "received from the Main Staff ... he sent it down to me and I sent to down to my units. That's how it went." And orders were unquestionable. When asked if he supported Mladic's decision that no man, woman, or child could leave besieged Vecici until those remaining there had surrendered their weapons, 22nd Brigade Battalion Commander Slobodan Zupljanin explained: "It wasn't up to me to support. It was up to me to implement the decisions -- implement the orders of my superior command." In paragraph 644 of its brief, the Defence claims Prosecution expert Butler gave evidence that the most important position in the VRS was corps commander. What Butler actually wrote at P2200, paragraph 2.0, was that corps commander was the most important position in a given VRS corps. The evidence shows the most important position in the VRS, the man responsible, was General Mladic. And, Your Honour, I see we're at the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 1.30 p.m. 12

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence claims in paragraph 646 that Mladic could not appoint corps or brigade commanders who it suggests were under Karadzic's control. And initially you can see Mladic appoint brigade commanders in P4985 and in his meeting with Svetozar Andric in Vlasenica on the 18th of May, 1992. And as Skrbic testified, VRS personnel decisions were drafted by the Main Staff's personnel sector based on Mladic's orders, even when they were for Karadzic to sign. But more fundamentally, Karadzic and Mladic worked together to implement the common purpose. Both repeatedly underscored the importance of unity between the military and political branches; what Gvero called the VRS's greatest value. That's P7391, page 3. And Karadzic, as Supreme Commander, recognised and relied on Mladic's essential role in the army's efforts. Milovanovic explained, for instance, that municipality President Dusko Kornjaca in Cajnice, a non-indictment municipality, had been the original brigade commander there and wanted to replace the commander who had been subsequently appointed pursuant to a Main Staff decision. When Milovanovic and then-Colonel Milenko Zivanovic complained to Karadzic, Karadzic called Kornjaca and he said: "Dusko, we are physicians. We don't know how to command in war. Let the professionals command." And that's how you see it working throughout the cleansing campaign. Karadzic meeting with Mladic, giving strategic direction, but letting the professionals command the army. As Karadzic put it in January 1994, he had "accepted entirely the decisions of all the officers and General Mladic." That's P4094, page 2. While Karadzic issued some specific orders, primarily later in the war, that was the exception, and there's certainly no evidence that Karadzic went around Mladic and the Main Staff to order VRS units to commit crimes without Mladic's knowledge. The Defence relies on Milovanovic's testimony that Karadzic issued him orders directly in August 1995 after the VRS had suffered a number of serious defeats in the Krajina. Now, Milovanovic says during that period, Karadzic gave him direct orders, and then Milovanovic explained: "All the orders that I received from him were forwarded by myself to General Mladic. And I waited for his position because Mladic was my immediate superior ..." At the very at least, he always Mladic informed. And that's at transcript page 16972 to 16973. Now this came long after Mladic and Karadzic had together used the VRS to ethnically cleanse most of BiH. And looking closer, this period shows the strength of Mladic's command. Even though Karadzic had attempted to reassign Mladic, Milovanovic ran Karadzic's orders by Mladic, his immediate superior, and five corps commanders signed a letter supporting Mladic; P4284. Mladic continued exercising command, and eventually Karadzic formally withdrew his decision, and they continued working together. Indeed, when the Defence discusses this in paragraph 3287 of their brief, they cite orders Mladic subsequently issued as Main Staff commander in the very next paragraph. This strong command and control was the way Mladic made his primary contribution to implementing the overarching JCE in this case. We set out his other contributions in paragraph 290 of our final brief. Now one of the messages Mladic ensured was disseminated down the chain of command was the JCE members' view that Bosnian Muslim and Croats generally were their enemies. Here we see Mladic instructing his subordinates what to do with their enemies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you are invited to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll try to accept, Mr. President. Mladic writes: "Keep pushing energetically onwards, pay no attention to what is going on around us. The Turks must disappear from these areas." And you see here the desire to expel being operationalized. And in an interview in the same year, 1994, Mladic explained many of the Bosnian Muslims were, as we'll see on the next slide, "not even Turks they are converts." The B/C/S word you see bolded is "Poturice" which you've heard is derogatory. And he calls them "the worst scum who had betrayed the Serb people." And this message was replayed down the VRS's ranks you see here P6647 and Defence witness Dragicevic, then the SRK's assistant commander for legal, morale and religious affairs, writing that Serbs were genetically superior to Muslims, stronger, better, more handsome and cleverer, and referring to them again as "Poturice." And we set out in paragraphs 72 through 82 of our brief the key role that Dragicevic's sector played in the propaganda campaign and disseminating the JCE members' message to soldiers on the ground. You see that this message throughout the VRS corps being repeated and operationalized. In 1st Krajina Corps chief of security Bogojevic's report on the removal of "the enemy," that is, the Muslim and Croat population of Kotor Varos. That's P3815. In 17th Brigade officer Marko Samardzija's reference to "the internal enemy, the Muslim population in our villages," that's P519. And in SRK commander Galic's exhortation to his soldiers that "the value of each individual and each unit is the measure to which they have safe-guarded the Serbs and Serbian territory and how many Poturice they have liquidated and how much of their territory they have seized." The VRS seized and ethnically cleansed the territory the JCE members had claimed. And, indeed, you see here how the Main Staff characterised the goals of its 1992 campaign in the combat readiness report. "Liberation of territories which are ours and which belong to us by historical birthright." The charged municipalities were all among those territories. And here we see again, P7325, page 2, Gvero's 19 May order. It reflects the Main Staff's view that the "state-building Serbian people living on around 65 per cent of the territory and representing around 35 per cent of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina must fight for a total partition from the Muslim and Croatian people and must create their own state." And you've heard from various Defence witnesses that this order implemented strategic objective 1 and told the soldiers the purpose of the war. That includes witness Barasin from the 1st Krajina Corps and Defence historic expert Kovic. And illustrated throughout our brief, Mladic knew very well how VRS units were pursuing "total partition." Indeed, he had to know in order to exercise command. The Chamber received the evidence of Mladic's detailed knowledge of VRS activities. 2nd Krajina Corps commander Boric explained Mladic "would know what the situation was like on the front line of the 2nd Krajina Corps without me having to report to him." And those reports meant Mladic "knew what was occurring in the entire AOR of the VRS." And that second reference is from P439. Now, the Defence attempts to undermine Mladic's knowledge of the notorious cleansing campaign by claiming in paragraph `665 that unless Mladic actively inquired about daily combat reports, he was not informed about them. This preposterous claim ignores that he chaired the Main Staff meetings at which such reports were discussed. It's from Milovanovic's testimony. It ignores East Bosnia Corps commander Simic's evidence that he spoke with Mladic almost every day to follow up on the daily combat report whether Mladic was in Crna Rijeka or out in the field. And that's P4325, transcript page 28494, and it ignores that even the witness they cite, Banduka, testified that -- testified not that the report didn't reach Mladic but that it went to the operative centre and as long as Mladic was present at Crna Rijeka "he would be conveyed that information from the operative centre of the Main Staff or the Chief of Staff himself." Consistent with Mladic's detailed knowledge about what his units were doing, he knew they were implementing his orders through the commission of widespread crimes. We noted in our brief, particularly at paragraphs 283 and 479, the international notoriety of the cleansing campaign. Many of the charged crimes were also individually notorious in Bosnia or outside it, and for the charged municipalities we set some of the evidence set out in the knowledge and approval sections of our municipality narratives. But, in short, the world was well aware of the nature of the cleansing campaign. Mladic must have known it too. He knew it from the international negotiators he met with, he knew it from the media, he knew it from meetings he recorded in his notebooks, and he knew it from daily combat reports that he received. Mladic received direct reports of crimes in some of those reports. The Defence notes this in paragraph 736 of its brief without giving any examples, but they claim that he received reports from the military justice system that those crimes were being prosecuted. I will get to the military justice system in a little while; but, for now, I want to make clear that there is nothing in its reports that suggests on even a cursory read that it was successfully prosecuting the perpetrators of crimes against non-Serbs. We set out a number of direct reports of crimes in our brief but just, for instance, you see Mladic's knowledge in P3733 where the 1 KK noted its "attempt to expel" Muslim and Croat refugees to Central Bosnia; or D418, where the 1 KK reported that "the Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village has been expelled." These reports documented just a few examples of how the VRS operationalized the JCE members' common purpose. The evidence shows that the VRS and other Bosnian Serb forces engaged in the same pattern of crimes throughout Serb-claimed territories. That pattern was present throughout the charged municipalities, in most of which the evidence we cited in our narratives and in our Scheduled Incident charts reflects that the cleansing campaign encompassed not just all the charged crimes but all the various persecutory acts charged in Count 3 of the indictment. And you also saw the pattern in evidence of Unscheduled Incidents which reinforce and corroborate the pattern of crimes, and the pattern reflects the organisation, preparation and planning that preceded these crimes. It reveals the common purpose behind them. The only reasonable inference from the pattern of grave and brutal crimes committed by Mladic's subordinates is that the crimes were part of the cleansing campaign's purpose. And you now see on your screen, or are about to, an order from General Mladic, a portion of Directive 4 reflecting the task he assigned to Drina Corps: "Exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on them and force them to leave the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas with the Muslim population." This is an unambiguous order to expel the Muslim population, an order for ethnic cleansing. That clear interpretation is confirmed by, among other things, the fact that the VRS implemented Directive 4 by expelling thousands of Bosnian Muslims from Eastern Bosnia. The history of Directive 4 which, as Mr. Tieger told you, arose from a meeting between Mladic and other high-level Bosnian Serb leaders where they discussed the need to "ciscenje" Eastern Bosnia. The implementing order Drina Corps commander Zivanovic issued, which explicitly orders Drina Corps units to expel the Muslim population and, finally, Mladic and other JCE members' goal of establishing a homogenous Serb Eastern Bosnia which had already been implemented through large-scale ethnic cleansing before Directive 4 was issued. You've heard evidence about how Directive 4 was implemented, and we address it particularly in paragraphs 401 through 412 of our brief. Systematic operations, ethnically cleansing one village at a time; P7361. Wanton destruction of Muslim hamlets around the Cerska enclave; P2193, P4093. And Drina Corps commander Zivanovic's call to his subordinates to do so: "Are the Turks' houses burning." Response: "They are burning, they are burning." And Zivanovic's: "Way to go, as many as possible." That's P2192. As Ibro Osmanovic's family reflects, many of those expelled had already been pushed from their homes to the remaining Muslim enclaves in Vlasenica and Bratunac, Cerska and Konjevic Polje. He testified: "My mother had been expelled from Vlasenica to Cerska. My sister was in Cerska. They were there until February 1993. From there, they passed through," and he mentions a number of other villages and then explains: "And they arrived Tuzla. The others, the remainder of the population went to Srebrenica. So Cerska was empty. It remained empty." And you see next Drina Corps commander Zivanovic's order implementing Directive 4, P2095, and he tells the Drina Corps he has decided pursuant to directive 4 to "inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde." So Zivanovic understood he was implementing an order to expel, to expel the population. The Defence relies in paragraph 2856 on General Milovanovic's self-serving claim that Directive 4 simply anticipated the Muslim population would flee. If that was the case, of course, Zivanovic wouldn't have needed to order them forced out and the conduct of the operations reflects, as you'd seen throughout the cleansing campaign, the goal was to expel them, the goal was to cleanse the territory. The Defence also claims in paragraph 2854 of its brief that Butler testified Directive 4 legitimately targeted a portion of the population which was assisting the Bosnian military. In fact, Butler testified that Directive 4 was unlawful and the VRS implemented it through targeting "the civilian population at large." And that's transcript pages 16135 to 16136 and 16144 to 16145. Directive 4 just put on paper the way the VRS conducted its operations from the time it was established. The systematic ethnic cleansing conducted in its implementation reflected what the VRS had already done throughout Serb-claimed territory. And so what it tells you is that the way the VRS fought the war - burning entire villages, expelling non-Serb civilians, and leaving them nothing to which return - was no accident. The directive merely codified long-term VRS practice under the name and signature of the man who had led the VRS in implementing the cleansing campaign from the establishment of the army, General Mladic. For instance, you see here P7086, an order by Birac Brigade commander Svetozar Andric on 26 May 1992 to "move women and children out of the Muslim villages to Kalesija and Gracanica, whereas the men are to be taken away to collection centres." Andric admitted that this meant women and children from Muslim villages had to move to Muslim-held territory. That's transcript page 34773. And you see here he was ordering his subordinates to move them. Realising the obvious implications of this order for ethnic cleansing, he attempted in testimony to claim this reference to women and children in Muslim villages was, in fact, a reference to women and children of all ethnicities before admitting at transcript page 34775 that the order specifically focused on moving out Muslim women and children. And you see here P7380 just over a month after Andric's cleansing order, Mladic promoting him to lieutenant-colonel. As you've heard and read, he ended the war a general and the Drina Corps Chief of Staff. Andric's order reflects that the cleansing operations and the roundup of non-Serbs during them created a need to warehouse huge numbers of prisoners, and the JCE members systemically detained them in terrible conditions, in camps where they were exposed to beatings, to sexual violence and where many were murdered. Now the camp system was a joint enterprise between the VRS, the RS MUP and Bosnian Serb civilian authorities. You see in P3801, Mico Stanisic's 17 July 1992 report that those institutions all shared responsibility for the system. He writes: "The army, Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible, and they leave such undefined camps to internal affairs organs. The conditions in some of these camps are poor; there is no food, individuals sometimes do not observe international norms, et cetera." The evidence shows many of these camps were run by internal affairs organs, as Stanisic said, but many of the charged camps were run by VRS units. And we set out in paragraphs 312 to 313 of our brief the evidence of the camp system was one single system, and following that the evidence of the terrible conditions throughout it. The VRS played a critical role in the system aside from leading the cleansing operations in which, as Stanisic noted, Muslim civilians were rounded up and captured, the VRS operated camps including the charged camps in Bijeljina, Banja Luka, Foca, Kalinovik, Rogatica and Trnopolje camp in Prijedor. Like in the rest of the system, the conditions in those camps were terrible. For the moment, I'm going to focus on two where the Defence concede the VRS ran the camps but claim conditions were humane. First, Batkovic was established in Bijeljina municipality at Mladic's order and operated by the East Bosnia Corps. The evidence shows it held thousands of non-Serb detainees in overcrowded and unsanitary conditions. Guards beat detainees, singled some out for particularly harsh treatment, killed several, and detainees were forced to beat and abuse each other. That's all in our Scheduled Incident chart. Just to look at one example, one witness was transferred from the Vlasenica prison to Batkovic on 13 August 1992 and held there until the 11 September 1992. He was one of ten detainees known as the special unit who were subjected to particularly cruel beatings and torture, beaten at least three times a day, ordered to beat each other and have sexual intercourse with each other. Often they were beaten in front of other prisoners. When journalists or Red Cross representatives came, the special unit members were hidden. And the injuries inflicted on this witness included a fractured skull, stab wounds in both hands and his left foot, cigarette burns, damage to his nervous system, fractures to his upper right arm, nose and jaw, broken ribs and damaged kidneys. So he had lasting physical injuries and post-traumatic stress. That's P2521 and P2522. Now, the Defence claims in paragraph 1629 of its brief that Batkovic legitimately held POWs and prisoners for whom there were suspicions that they committed criminal acts or war crimes. The very evidence they cite refutes this. They cite first P3806, which refers to the transfer of prisoners from Manjaca. As I'll get to in a moment, the prisoners held there were known mostly to be simple civilians. And for the second discussion, can we briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Defence witness and military judge Bojanovic admitted he visited Muslim civilians detained at Batkovic. That's transcript page 27975. And Defence witness Andan admitted a Croat he knew was being detained at Batkovic only because he was a Croat. "I couldn't find any other reason or explanation." The Defence claim that transferring prisoners to Batkovic for exchange "proves the VRS had no criminal intent" - that's in paragraph 1641 of their brief is unsubstantial - is unsustainable. Those people being held to be exchanged out of Serb territory because of their ethnicity were held by the VRS in criminal, disgraceful conditions, were primarily civilians who had been rounded up to be detained and eventually removed and were abused and some killed in detention. Turning to Manjaca, the 1st Krajina Corps held thousands of detainees there, almost all non-Serbs. They were held with insufficient food and water, in crowded stables, many were severely beaten and otherwise abused and at least ten killed. For instance, a judge from Sanski Most who was transferred from Manjaca on 17 June 1992. He was beaten regularly, beginning as soon as he arrived. He fainted several times during beatings by soldiers and military police, lost a tooth, lost approximately one-third of his body weight due to the lack of food in the camp before being transferred to Germany in December 1992. He was still suffering pain from the beatings when he gave a statement in 2000. That's P3293. The Defence claim that the VRS released detainees who were found not to have participated in combat is also based on Manjaca evidence. That evidence, P241, shows 700 Manjaca detainees being transferred to Croatia in November 1992, thus completing their permanent removal from Serb-claimed territory. The Defence witness Solaja admitted the Bosnian Serb leadership had made a condition of closing the camp. The other evidence they rely on, P219, simply refers to the intention to "discuss the possibility" of some detainees' returning home, but they cite no examples of anyone who did, perhaps because the VRS had destroyed many of the Muslim homes and villages in Sanski Most during its cleansing operations as we set out in our municipality narrative. Here, too, the evidence shows the prisoners being held by the VRS at Manjaca were civilians. In the main, I'd refer you to P220, P221, and the evidence of Adil Medic that 1st Krajina Corps officer Vukelic had told him very few of the detainees at Manjaca had anything to do with the armed conflict. In paragraph 62 of its brief, the Defence dispute what they call Pyers Tucker's "hearsay evidence" that Mladic controlled detention facilities, including Batkovic, KP Dom Foca and Kula prison. First, the evidence is that Mladic himself told Tucker that he controlled those facilities. That's not hearsay evidence; it's an admission. Second, in Kula, the Defence also ignore the testimony of their own witness, Main Staff officer Savo Sokanovic, that Kula prison was "under the control of the army." As we set out in our Ilidza narrative, VRS officers, including members of the SRK command, exercised such control, in part, by approving the use of Kula prison detainees for forced labour on the front lines where some were killed. The Defence claims that this was done by individuals acting against orders, but the very documents that they cite in footnote 3058 of their brief reflect VRS officers, including SRK chief of security Marko Lugonja, approving these forced labour assignments. And Kula was one of the hubs of the detention camp system, like Batkovic and Foca and Manjaca. The Defence argues in paragraph 1324 that "a 156 people" were accommodated at Kula, only combatants when Bosnian Serb documentation, for instance, P3808 reflects that thousands of non-Serb civilians had passed through Kula by October 1994. We set out in paragraphs 322 through 332 of our brief just some of the evidence that huge numbers of civilians were detained throughout the camp system, consistent with the practice at Batkovic, Manjaca, and Kula and with the Andric order that you saw earlier. Now, one of the places the intentional detention of civilians is most apparent is in the processing of Manjaca prisoners in late August 1992, after international condemnation of the Bosnian Serb camps. Mladic met with the Presidency and then the Main Staff tasked the Manjaca camp staff with processing detainees. The camp identified 92 who did not participate in combat activities, also had serious health problems, and were attracting the attention of journalists and representatives of humanitarian organisations. You see that in P4288 and you see the criteria at page 1. You can see in this still from a BBC broadcast, P243, that such prisoners were attracting international attention. But three weeks later, only three of the 92 prisoners the camp staff had identified were released pursuant to pardons from President Karadzic, and you see other evidence that the 1 KK was detaining known civilians there, for instance, in paragraph 341 of our brief. Finally, for today I want to turn to the Defence attempt to undermine the evidence of the individual charged crimes. The Defence suggests for various crimes that crimes were committed by drunk soldiers acting on their own or that civilians wearing military uniforms on the same day the VRS attacked a village committed crimes in that village during the attack and somehow the VRS didn't notice. Now, we set out in the Scheduled Incident charts in our brief the evidence which, considered in its totality, conclusively identifies perpetrators. In various incidents, that evidence includes VRS reports showing units attacking villages on the date of the charged crime, includes witnesses familiarity with their tormentors which enabled them to identify perpetrators by name or unit, includes the use of heavy military weaponry, like tanks, and is supported by the ability of witnesses from a society with compulsory military service to distinguish between different types of uniforms. I want to look at one such incident specifically, the cleansing of Novoseoci village in Sokolac municipality, Scheduled Incident A8.1 Crisis Staff president Milan Tupajic explained that the 2nd Romanija Brigade surrounded and blocked Novoseoci on the evening of 21 September 1992. That's P3170, transcript page 15428. This followed brigade commander Radislav Krstic's order the day before to attack areas in Sokolac municipality, P6641, which itself implemented SRK commander Galic's order, P7408. Now survivor, Munira Selmanovic explained on 22 September 1992 she saw soldiers dressed in olive-drab and camouflage uniforms in Novoseoci who rounded up the Muslim villagers and brought them to Metaljka field. That's P717, paragraph 8. And she recognised Momcilo Pajic, a Serb she knew very well, was in charge of the soldiers. That's paragraphs 11 and 12. Your Honours see who Pajic was on this document: A captain and military police commander in the 2nd Romanija Brigade, the same unit Tupajic mentioned until he was promoted here to major in 1995. Pajic told Selmanovic -- And, Your Honour, I have about two minutes on this point if it would all right for everyone to finish the topic for continuity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would limit it to two minutes, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Pajic told Selmanovic and the others gathered at the field to wait while he went to Sokolac for orders. When he returned, at his order, the soldiers separated men from women, children and elderly people. Selmanovic and the other women, children, and elderly people were taken to the confrontation lines and dropped off, then walked into besieged Sarajevo. She begged to take her teenage son with her, but he was kept at Metaljka field. The 2nd Romanija Brigade, you will see on the next slide, reported to the Main Staff that evening at 1800 hours that it had "ciscenje" the village of Novoseoci that day. By the evening, Tupajic knew the men had been murdered. That's P3170, transcript pages 15427 and 15428. He, Selmanovic, P727, and P7529 reflect that the victims were then buried in a garbage dump at a place called Ivan Polje, and the exhumation report for the site, P727, shows you the victims were the same people Selmanovic saw surrounded and detained by soldiers, left behind at the field. Tupajic's evidence that the men were murdered is borne out by the forensic evidence, P2262, which shows the people in the grave site died of gunshot wounds mostly multiple times from behind with high-velocity rifles. And you can see here the remains of the Novoseoci mosque blown up the same day by 2nd Romanija Brigade engineers found in the garbage pile on top of the mass grave, and the slide is P2512, page 18, and the same information is in P727 and at transcript page 6818. So the evidence fits together like a mosaic to prove the crime and the identify of the perpetrators. I thank Your Honours for your indulgence, and I'll pick up tomorrow morning.
